doc.title: Mike Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2024

title: Explaining improvisation to a non-musician
summary: After a remark on a Burghausen video, Davis likens improvisation to Mozartian counterpoint played on the fly.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I watched a video of you playing “Waiting on a Friend” at the Burghausen Fest, and I will have to say that’s an impressive display of sackbut ability.
Well you’re very kind Monk, thank you. Yeah some days I feel like I can get around the thing and other days I’m trying to figure it out still.

Well that leads me to — what are you — let’s put it this way, if you met somebody who is not a musician, like my father used to be so confused by what are they doing. He’d hear somebody that was clearly improvising and I couldn’t — at the time I can’t remember what I said to him. But can you succinctly explain to someone just a kernel of what improvising is?

I probably won’t be very succinct but I’ll try anyway. Yeah I think of it as you know the thing I would draw the closest parallel to might be if you listen to a Mozart symphony you’re going to hear melody, you’re going to hear harmony, and then you’re going to hear counterpoint, which is material that is supplementing and complementing the melody and the harmony. And that’s all written down in an orchestral composition. But to me, you know we talked about Charlie Parker earlier. Charlie Parker, his improvisation is basically the same as Mozart counterpoint except that he’s doing it on the fly. He’s not writing it down, he’s not — he hasn’t necessarily prepared it although I think jazz musicians develop a vocabulary that they’re comfortable using. That’s why any of us can hear Charlie Parker and know right away it’s Charlie Parker. Or you can hear right away that it’s Mike Rodriguez or pick whoever you like. So to me I guess I’ve already crossed the line of being succinct but to me it’s really, it’s counterpoint. It’s that element of the music that you’re used to hearing in a symphony or in anything — in rock & roll too. Maybe they wouldn’t break it down in the same way but there’s kind of those three or

four elements and the one element in jazz that is counterpoint is an improvised solo that’s happening in real time. You’re not writing down anything, you’re not playing exactly what you prepared, you’re reacting to the other players and the other input you’re getting from the other players as opposed to a written symphony. But conceptually it’s kind of the same kind of material.
